sections.html:
There is no second layer of local government in Denver County. On December 1, 1902 the City of Denver merged with Arapahoe County, creating one consolidated city and county that covers 154.7 square miles. Its 78 official neighborhoods grew out of the 1970 statistical neighborhoods, and well-known informal names such as LoDo, RiNo, Park Hill and Central Park, the former Stapleton area, are used alongside them.

You receive a single tax bill here, and the people who value and collect work in the same Department of Finance. The bill lists each taxing authority on your parcel. Two houses a short walk apart may sit in different school or special districts.

Value comes from the Assessor and collection from the Treasury division. Neither sets the rate. If a bill seems too high, decide whether the value is off, which the Assessor can review, or the levy is simply high, which only the taxing authority controls.

OfficeWhat it does
Assessor's OfficeValues real property, mails Notices of Valuation, takes protests
TreasuryMails statements, collects payments, runs the delinquent list and tax lien sale
Taxing authoritiesSet mill levies each December

Denver's combined general levy for 2024 was 79.202 mills, or 0.079202.

Appraisers compare each house with recent sales of similar homes, and the whole city gets a new appraisal every second year, the odd-numbered ones such as 2023 and 2025. The 2025 values rest on sales from July 1, 2022 through June 30, 2024. Commercial and industrial property uses cost, market and income approaches, and business personal property is valued from what owners declare.

The Assessor's formula: (actual value minus value reduction) times assessment rate times mill levy. For 2024 the inputs were:

  • Residential: $55,000 value reduction per parcel, 6.7% assessment rate.
  • Commercial improved: $30,000 reduction, 27.9% rate.
  • All other: no reduction, 27.9% rate.

Residential property now carries two rates, and the state's 2026 chart lists 6.8% for local government levies and 7.05% for school levies. Your own notice and bill hold the numbers for the year you are in.

Expect your statement in January. You can pay half by the last day of February and half by June 15, or pay in full by April 30.

  • By May 1: the Assessor mails Notices of Valuation.
  • May: delinquency notices go to unpaid accounts.
  • September and October: delinquent taxes are advertised in a local newspaper.
  • October: the public auction of real estate tax liens.

The Assessor mails senior citizen and disabled veteran exemption notices in January. Elderly and disabled refund applications are due April 30, and deferral applications for seniors and active-duty military are due April 1.

File by June 8, or the next business day when that date is a weekend or holiday. Instructions arrive with the Assessor's Notice of Valuation, and protests can be written, made in person or sent over the internet. Your protest should have:

  • Your parcel or schedule number from the notice and a daytime phone number.
  • Your reasons, stated plainly.
  • Evidence such as comparable sales or documented condition problems.

Let a year slip by? You can reach back two prior years with a Board of County Commissioners petition for abatement or refund of taxes. A decision you dislike can go to the State Board of Assessment Appeals, to District Court or to binding arbitration. Counties with more than 300,000 residents follow the state's alternate schedule, with Notices of Determination mailed by August 15.

Filing before you list can help. A lower value changes the bill your buyer takes over, and a house with documented repair needs usually argues its case better than one in move-in shape.

Storms are frequent enough that the roof is normally the first thing a buyer or inspector brings up. Denver ranks tenth among U.S. cities of 50,000 or more for hail risk, and three of the ten costliest hailstorms in U.S. history struck it, in 1990, 2009 and 2017.

Hail scars, cracked siding and dented gutters cut into a conventional buyer's offer. Selling to a cash buyer who accepts the house as is takes that haggling off the table.

Denver lists several relief programs on its calendar. Senior citizen and disabled veteran exemption notices come from the Assessor in January. The elderly and disabled refund program takes applications until April 30. Seniors and active-duty military can apply for a deferral by April 1, and anyone who is planning to sell should read the repayment terms before applying.

The state records a deferral against the house as a lien. A sale adds its payoff to the closing statement, so request the amount while the house is listed and not the day before you close.

With a buyer under contract, things move fast. Title orders the payoff and searches for liens, and whatever turns up is itemized for closing. The buyer's money clears the tax, any liens and your mortgage, and you get what is left. After that the deed is filed and the account passes to the new owner.

Gather your latest statement, Notice of Valuation and any protest papers before you call the title officer. Tell the buyer about a protest that is still open, because a change in value will land on them rather than you.

If you are unsure whether you ever claimed an exemption, call the Assessor and ask what is on file for the parcel. A missing exemption is easier to fix before a sale than after one. Ask the Treasury about service liens at the same time, so one round of phone calls covers every balance that could show up on the settlement statement, and you can plan your closing date around real numbers.

sections.h2: If you owe tax and want to sell
sections.html:
Start by finding the exact amount, since a delinquent balance gathers interest and may be sold as a tax lien. Treasury publishes a delinquent real property list and takes questions at propertytaxinfo@denvergov.org, where you should send your parcel ID, address and payment dates if a notice looks wrong.

  • Get the live balance in hand before listing or signing a contract.
  • Find out if earlier years are still open, not just the current one.
  • Look for service liens, which Treasury handles too.
  • Mention the debt to any buyer up front so closing can absorb it.

Cash deals can close quickly, with the tax paid from proceeds just like a mortgage payoff, which stops the account from slipping further while you decide. On a regular listing the title company requests the figure, prints it on the settlement statement and sends the money to Treasury when the deed records.

faqs.q: What is the property tax protest deadline in Denver County?
faqs.a: June 8 each year. When June 8 falls on a weekend or holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day, and the Notice of Valuation explains how to file.

faqs.q: How often does Denver reappraise homes?
faqs.a: Once every two years, in odd-numbered years. The 2025 values drew on sales between July 1, 2022 and June 30, 2024.

faqs.q: Who sets the tax rate in Denver?
faqs.a: Taxing authorities set the mill levies in December. The Assessor neither sets rates nor collects money. The 2024 combined general levy in Denver was 79.202 mills.

faqs.q: When are Denver property taxes due?
faqs.a: Half payments are due the last day of February and June 15, and full payment is due April 30.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Denver house if the taxes are unpaid?
faqs.a: Yes. The balance comes out of your sale proceeds. Ask Treasury for the current amount first, so closing holds no surprises.
